comment: Compiled to per-material GPU buckets at load (hot-reload with R). chance is per-mille per 30 Hz tick. Rules for the same self are tried in file order and at most ONE fires per cell per tick — put specific rules (acid+stone) before generic tag rules (acid+tag:dissolvable). Three shapes: pair {self,neighbor,...}, decay {self,decay:true,becomes}, emit {self,emit,dir}. neighbor accepts a material id, tag:xxx, or any (optionally filtered by neighborClass). dir: any|up|down|side. Products: selfBecomes/neighborBecomes/becomes; 'air' deletes.

reactions.note: -------- fire: short-lived rising flame; doused by water --------
-------- smoke & steam: fade; steam condenses into rain --------

-------- combustion: each flammable defines its burn character --------
THE IGNITION CHANCE IS HOW FAST FIRE SPREADS THROUGH THE FUEL; the decay rules further down are how long a lit voxel takes to be consumed. They are separate levers and this note exists because they are easy to confuse. Wood/bark were slowed 1.5x here (18 -> 12, birch 22 -> 15, staff 16 -> 11) so a fire creeps up a trunk instead of running it; the ember decays below are UNCHANGED, so a lit log still burns out on the same schedule it always did.

foliage flashes to fire and is CONSUMED (no ember stage): a burning canopy should vanish in flame, not decay into thousands of ash voxels raining through the crown. Chances are high because leaves are thin fuel; the burn is bounded by the canopy itself (fire decays in ~6 ticks and leaves nothing that grows). ALL FOLIAGE CHANCES WERE CUT 3x on owner report that a crown went up too readily (leaves 225->75->25, needles 380->127, autumn 400->133): a tree should catch and take a while about it rather than flashing over the instant an ember touches it. The RATIOS between the three fuels are preserved -- dry needles and dead autumn leaf still catch several times faster than green leaves, which is the read that makes a pine forest frightening and an oak wood merely flammable.

THE SHADE RAMPS BURN LIKE WHAT THEY ARE. assets/editor/treegen.js bakes each foliage and bark family as a three-material ramp (dark / plain / lit) so a crown has form; combustion in this file is authored BY NAME, not by tag, so a ramp member with no rule of its own is a leaf that will not catch. Same chance as its plain sibling in every case -- these are lighting tiers, not different fuels, and a canopy that burned in stripes would be worse than one that did not burn at all.
-------- ember: smolders, licks flame upward, dies to ash; doused back to charwood --------

The ember stage IS the burn: wood ignites to ember on contact with tag:hot, then smolders here until one of these decay rules retires it. Their SUM is the death rate, so scaling all three together sets burn DURATION without touching how fire spreads (that is the wood+tag:hot ignition rule above, deliberately left fast). Total 7 per-mille vs the old 27 = wood takes ~4x longer to be consumed, ~140 ticks mean. Within that budget ash is ~1/4 of decays and smoke is doubled relative to the old 20:7 ash:smoke split, so a burnt-out fire leaves a scatter of ash rather than a floor of it. Embers also live 4x longer, so each one emits its upward fire ~4x more over its life: fire persists longer without spreading faster.

"burnDuration": true MARKS A RULE AS PART OF THE COMBUSTION CLOCK. Every marked chance is divided by combustion.burnDurationPct at load (src/sim/materials.cpp), so the Combustion tab is one slider over how long anything in the world stays alight, authored once here rather than by hand-editing eighteen chances that have to keep their ratios.

Two kinds of rule carry it, and the second is not obvious. The first is every rule that RETIRES a burning voxel -- ember to ash, smoke or air; burning cloth, undercloth, hair and flesh to their spent forms. Halving those is the feature.

The second is every RELIGHT rule (charred back to burning). Those are the only rules in the file that put matter BACK into a burning state, so they are the only closed loop in the fire economy, and its gain is (relight chance per tick) x (how long a neighbour stays lit). Scaling the burn duration without scaling these multiplies that gain by the same factor, which is fine at 200% -- measured, the difference at the `mob-burn` corpse was 13 voxels still alight versus 15, i.e. nothing -- and is not fine at the top of the slider, where an unscaled gain would cross 1.0 and the fire would never go out (CLAUDE.md rule 2). This is a CEILING argument, not a fix for anything observed at the default: dividing the relight rules too holds the gain exactly where the author put it at every setting, so the slider changes the CLOCK of the fire and never its shape. A corpse in lava re-flares half as often and stays lit twice as long, which is the same corpse running at half speed.

It is NOT on the ignition rules, the emit rules or the extinguisher rules, and each exclusion is a decision: ignition is how fast fire SPREADS (a separate lever -- see the combustion note at the top of this file -- and leaving it alone is what makes a longer burn also spread further, since a voxel that stays lit twice as long emits its upward flame twice as many times), emit is how much flame a lit voxel SHOWS, and dousing must beat the burn to the tick at any setting.
-------- water vs heat --------
-------- lava: crusts against water, melts sand. Deliberately NOT tag:meltable: glass must be stable next to lava or the pool rim remelts its own crust forever and never sleeps --------
-------- molten glass: cools to glass, quenched instantly by water --------
-------- acid erosion chain (stone->gravel->sand->gone); glass is immune --------

ACID EATS MEAT FAR FASTER THAN IT EATS ROCK, and this is the rule that says so. Ordered BEFORE the generic tag:dissolvable rule below, per the file's specific-before-generic convention, so mineral erosion keeps its old slow chain and only organics get the fast one.

WHY IT MATTERS OUT OF PROPORTION TO ITS SIZE: this rule reaches a BODY. mob.cpp's inbound pass evaluates acid's own rules FROM the grid cell ONTO each body voxel it touches (the same direction the GPU evaluates them), so skin, flesh, bone, cloth and leather -- all tag:organic -- are eaten by this line and by nothing that had to be written for them. At the old shared 45 per-mille a limb at skinScale 8 lost about 4.5% of ONE sub-voxel layer per tick, roughly two seconds per layer and the better part of a minute for an arm, which is what 'acid does not do nearly enough damage' actually was. At 250 a layer goes in about ten ticks.

Steel is unaffected because `steel` carries no tag:organic and no tag:dissolvable -- armour still protects, and still for the reason equipment.h states: not a resist number, an absence of the tag.
-------- cold: creeping freeze, melting, snow compaction --------
-------- plants: the sandspiel signature. plant grows into water; seeds sprout stalks that race hardening vs growth; stems rarely branch; tips bloom --------
germination is daylight-only (day/night cycle). The chance is unchanged, so a seed sown in the morning behaves exactly as before; one sown at night simply waits for dawn.

stem growth must stay decisively subcritical: mean stalk = up/(up-decays) cells, branches-per-stalk = stalk * side/(side+decays). At 380/4/78 that is ~6-cell stalks with R~0.3 branches — the epidemic dies out and chunks sleep. Raising side or up can make growth self-sustaining forever (measured: 400/6/52 never settles).
-------- fungus: creeps over everything organic --------
-------- mites: wandering critters — eat the garden, breed on plants, drown, expire --------
-------- cloner-style sources and the void drain --------
blood dries away so pools go back to sleep (PLAN #B5, rule 2)

======== DAY/NIGHT INTERACTIONS ========================================
These carry the light conditions added with the day/night cycle:
  "needsSky": true   the cell must have open sky above it (bounded probe up)
  "when": "day"      only while the sun is up  |  "night" only while it is down
  "minLight": 0-255  a floor on daylight strength (255 = only at high noon)

All three are integer and derived from the tick-based day phase, so they are
as deterministic as every other rule (CLAUDE.md rule 1).

SLEEP DISCIPLINE (rule 2): a rule whose light condition is UNMET does not hold
its chunk awake, so a pond sleeps all night instead of spinning. The engine
wakes every chunk on the tick daylight switches on or off (Simulation::
EncodeWakeAll), which is a few ticks per in-game day. Chances are kept low so
these are a slow background weathering, not a strobe.

-------- sun + water: evaporation --------
SPREAD WATER burns off in the sun; BODIES of water do not. This is the mirror
image of the freezing rule below, and it is the whole reason evaporation is
interesting rather than just a slow leak on every pond.

The chance is scaled by how many of the six face neighbours are NOT water
("neighbor": "water" + "invert": true), with a minCount of 4 — so a cell needs
to be mostly OUT of the water before the sun can take it:

  - 0 non-water (deep water)               never. Fully enclosed.
  - 1 non-water (flat pond surface, air     never. This is the case that
    above and water on all five other       matters: a pond's surface is NOT
    sides)                                  consumed, so ponds are stable.
  - 2-3 non-water (surface near a bank)    never. Still reads as "pond".
  - 4 non-water (a rim cell, a thin sheet) base rate, ~1 real minute.
  - 5 non-water (nearly isolated)          1.3x
  - 6 non-water (a lone droplet on stone)  3x, ~40 real seconds.

So rain puddles and splash thrown onto hot rock steam away while the lake they
came from sits there. Because a pond can only ever lose cells from its rim,
and losing a rim cell exposes the next one, a SHALLOW puddle still dries up
from its edges inward — it just takes minutes, not seconds.

minLight 120 confines it to the middle of the day (the rule is live for about
a quarter of the cycle), and needsSky keeps water in caves and under canopy
intact. Strictly consumptive (water -> steam -> mostly air), so it is
subcritical by construction: it can only ever remove water.

-------- steam condenses into rain --------
Steam already decays to water at 3 per mille everywhere. This adds a NIGHT
bias: cold night air condenses it faster, so morning fog burns off and evening
air turns to dew. Still net-consumptive of steam.

-------- snow and ice follow the sun --------
Snow in direct sun melts; exposed water freezes on clear nights. These two are
opposed, which is exactly what makes them safe: they cannot both fire in the
same phase, so there is no melt/freeze loop that keeps chunks awake. The ice
rule needs sky so lakes freeze from the top and cave water stays liquid, and it
is scaled by neighbour count so a pond freezes shore-first — see the note on
the water rule below.

Ice grows from the SHORE inward, it does not flash-freeze the pond.
The chance is scaled by how many of the six face neighbours are NOT water
("neighbor": "water" + "invert": true), which produces the real behaviour for
free:

  - Deep interior water is surrounded by water: count 0, chance 0, it CANNOT
    freeze. No ice ever nucleates in open water.
  - Water touching the bank, or the pond surface (the cell above is air), has
    count >= 1 and freezes at the base rate.
  - Every voxel that DOES freeze becomes ice, which is itself non-water, so it
    raises its liquid neighbours' count and their odds. The front feeds itself
    and creeps inward.
  - A cell in a narrow channel, nearly enclosed by bank and ice, hits count 6
    and freezes at scaleMax (4x).

This is decisively subcritical (rule 2) despite being self-reinforcing: it
converts water and water does not come back at night, so the frontier is a
shrinking 2D surface that terminates when the pond is solid. The day rule above
melts it back, and the two cannot fire in the same phase.

-------- growth follows the light --------
Plants only put on growth in daylight. The existing stem/sprout rules are left
alone (their subcritical budget is carefully tuned — see the stem note above);
these are the ADDITIONAL daylight-only behaviours.

Grass creeping onto lit soil is the one rule here that creates new matter, so
it is the one to watch: it is capped by needsSky (only the exposed top surface
of the ground qualifies) and by requiring a soil neighbour, so the frontier is
a 2D surface, not a volume, and it terminates when the surface is covered. At
3 per mille it spreads about a cell per 10 in-game seconds of daylight.

flowers close at night and reopen by day (petal <-> flower is a pure
palette swap between two inert solids, so it cannot cascade)

-------- fungus prefers the dark --------
The existing fungus rule spreads over organics at 7 per mille regardless of
light. This adds a faster NIGHT spread, so a cellar or a moonlit forest floor
creeps visibly while a sunlit meadow barely does. Same bounded frontier as the
existing rule (it converts organics, and organics do not regrow).

-------- sunlight through glass ignites tinder --------
The magnifying-glass trick. Requires the dry foliage to be under open sky AND
touching glass AND near peak sun, so it is rare enough to be a discovery
rather than a hazard that burns the world down every noon. Fire is already
bounded (it decays in ~6 ticks and leaves nothing that regrows).

-------- NOT IMPLEMENTED: overnight dew on foliage --------
A night-time "leaves emit steam upward" rule was tried twice and REMOVED both
times. Recording it here so it is not re-attempted a third time.

Attempt 1 — plain emit. doReactions() set keepAwake as soon as an emit rule
found an adjacent air cell, before rolling its chance, so every leaf with air
above it pinned its chunk awake all night: 292/32768 chunks active after 2900
settle ticks, against a budget of 32 (CLAUDE.md rule 2).

Attempt 2 — after making light-gated rules skip keepAwake (that change was
kept; it is correct and the other gated rules need it). Still 250 chunks
awake, now as a permanent steam plume: every canopy leaf is a SOURCE, the
steam it emits is a gas that moves every tick and re-dirties its chunk, and
emission outpaces steam's decay. Awake chunks were a vertical column at fixed
x,z — a plume, not a settling neighbourhood.

The lesson is rule 2's: a permanent emitter has no terminus, so no chance
value makes it settle. Dew needs a FINITE source — e.g. a dew material that
leaves deposit once and consume, or a decay on something that runs out.
Left out rather than shipped breaking the sleep guarantee.
-------- BODIES: per-voxel burning (docs/PLAN_body_reactivity.md) --------

These materials only ever exist as MOB and ITEM geometry, so until now they were tagged flammable and had no rules at all: a creature could stand in a bonfire forever. Nothing below is mob-specific. MobSystem::BurnLimbs and DebrisSystem::BurnBodies run this same authored table over body voxels through the CPU mirror in sim/reactcpu.h, so a burning limb, a severed burning arm, a dropped burning staff and a robe_cloth voxel that settled into the grid all behave identically.

THE SHAPE OF THE MECHANIC. Cloth catches from ONE hot neighbour at about 8x flesh's rate; flesh does not catch at all until THREE of its six faces are hot. That is authored as a decay rule with scaleByNeighbors, because a pair rule's neighbour fields are already spoken for by its partner. The minCount is the load-bearing number: it is what makes a lone ember on a shoulder gutter out while a wide burning front races, i.e. the difference between 'the mob is on fire' as a boolean and fire as a front with a width.

CLOTH: catches from a single hot face and is CONSUMED, leaving holes and scorched rag. All three robe materials share one burning state so the burn character is authored once and a new fabric inherits it by naming cloth_burning as its product.
Leather is fabric that resists: the same burning state at one eighth the catch rate. The whole 'a leather jerkin buys you seconds a robe does not' mechanic is this one number.

Douse FIRST, then emit, then the decays -- the ember ordering, for the ember reason: water must beat the burn to the tick, and a voxel that spent its tick licking flame upward should not also consume itself. Total decay 39 per-mille is about 26 ticks (0.9 s) per cloth voxel, so a robe burns away over seconds instead of vanishing in one frame.

The ash branch is deliberately 15x rarer than it first shipped (5 -> 0.33 per-mille): a burning robe is a lot of voxels and at 5 per-mille it buried the wearer's feet in ash. Its old share went to the 'becomes air' branch so the 39 per-mille total -- and therefore the burn DURATION -- is unchanged; only the fraction of cloth that survives as matter moved. Ash from a garment is now a scatter, not a pile.
Charred rag is spent fuel: three hot faces to relight, so a burnt-out garment does not smoulder its wearer to death after the fire is over.
HAIR: catches almost on contact and is gone in about 4 ticks. One material and three rules, and it is the clearest single read that a character is on fire.

-------- UNDERCLOTH: the base human's linen, which BLACKENS AND STAYS --------
A near-copy of the cloth chain above with one branch deleted, and the deletion is the mechanic. cloth_burning is CONSUMED (26.67 of its 39 per-mille go to air), which is right for a robe -- a burnt robe should hang in rags. It is wrong for the one garment the character is wearing UNDER everything: burning it away undresses them, and 'the player caught fire and is now naked' is a worse read than any amount of scorching.

So undercloth_burning has exactly one decay branch and it lands on undercloth_charred, which authors no rules at all. Same 39 per-mille total, so it burns for the same LENGTH of time as a robe and responds to the burn-duration slider identically; only the destination moved. It still catches at cloth's rate, still emits fire upward while alight, so it still spreads a fire and still cooks the flesh underneath through the ordinary table -- what it cannot do is disappear.

FLESH: sears on contact, ignites only under a WIDE front. skin -> flesh_cooked is a plain pair rule, so a single lick of flame cooks the surface and a creature can be seared without being destroyed. Ignition is the scaled decay below.

IGNITION WAS RAISED 9.75x IN TWO PASSES (40 -> 130 -> 390) on owner report that a body was not flammable enough. THE SEAR WAS NOT, and the attempt to raise it is worth recording because it was wrong for a reason that is easy to repeat: skin -> flesh_cooked is a COLOUR CHANGE, not combustion, so raising it makes a body look cooked faster without making it any more likely to catch. It also broke the one comparison this whole section is built on -- at sear 220 vs cloth's 200 the flesh reacted to a single hot face MORE eagerly than the cloth over it, which inverts 'cloth catches at about 8x flesh's rate' -- and the mob-burn gate caught it as cloth and skin halving on the same tick. Flammability is the decay below; the sear stays at 90. THE MINCOUNT DID NOT MOVE and must not: 3 is the reason a lone ember on a shoulder gutters out, and it is provable rather than tuned (see the next note). At 390 with scaleMax 4 the scaled chance is 858 per-mille at the minCount-3 threshold and saturates at 1000 under a full six-face front, i.e. cooked flesh under a real fire ignites within a tick or two -- the SEAR (90) is now what paces a body catching alight, not the ignition. Raising the chance makes a real fire take hold quickly; lowering the count would make ANY spark take hold, which is a different and much worse game.

minCount 3 is deliberate and provable: a lone burning voxel plus the single fire cell it emits reach 2, so one ignited voxel cannot restart itself no matter how the dice fall. Three simultaneously hot faces means a real fire -- or burning cloth lying against the skin, which is exactly how a clothing layer is supposed to kill you.

Burning flesh almost always CHARS IN PLACE rather than disappearing: charred is a solid, so the limb keeps its shape and reads as burnt instead of eaten away. That is what leaves a recognisable blackened corpse -- and, where a limb burned through, bone, which has no fire rules at all and therefore survives by construction.

The ash branch takes the same 15x cut as cloth's above (8 -> 0.53 per-mille) and for the same reason, with its old share folded into the char branch so the 50 per-mille total and the burn duration are unchanged. Burning bodies still shed ash, just rarely enough that it reads as soot rather than as the body dissolving into a heap.

DEEP CHAR. flesh_charred is what one pass of flame leaves: dark, but still brown and still meat. Fire that KEEPS coming takes it one stage further to flesh_cinder -- near-black, crisp, and inert. That is the difference between 'this body was in a fire' and 'this body was torched', and it is a stage rather than a palette jitter because it has different RULES: cinder authors none at all, so it can neither re-ignite nor be driven further, and a corpse burned this far is permanently black and permanently settled.

It sits ABOVE the relight rule on purpose. Both roll every tick on the same voxel and the first to fire wins, so at 20 vs 8 a body under a sustained blaze cinders about two and a half times more often than it flares back up. That makes the char chain CONVERGE under fire instead of cycling charred -> burning -> charred, which is strictly better for rule 2 than the relight rule alone: the terminus is an inert material rather than a coin flip that never ends.

minCount 3 rather than the relight rule's 4 because this is a much smaller claim -- 'the fire is still on me', not 'the fire is hot enough to restart spent fuel' -- and because a lone ember still cannot reach 3 (see the minCount note above). Not marked burnDuration: nothing here is alight, so the burn-duration slider has no business in it.

Charred flesh relights only under a full four-face front, which in practice means lava or a sustained blaze. Without that floor a burnt corpse is a permanent low-grade emitter and its chunk never sleeps (CLAUDE.md rule 2).
A dropped wooden staff is a debris body with a micro brick and BurnBodies runs this table over it, so 'fire lights the item you dropped' costs exactly this one rule.
